E555 · Stage B · fixed-frame corpus

Which pieces belong near which corner

55,712 partial boards from 1,741 independent border configurations, harvested from four sides of one pinned frame. None of them solves anything. The question is whether the pinned corners and clues bend the placement distribution hard enough to be worth exploiting — and whether exploiting it actually helps.

The preferences are real and the ranking works. Twelve pieces is far too many to remove.

Where pieces belong is strongly and reproducibly structured: two independent views of each corner agree at ρ = +0.701, against +0.006 under a label shuffle. Barring the twelve far-side pieces from the chain database nevertheless made the search much worse, not better. the exclusion HURTS: at row 10 the frontier is 0.03x as wide [0.03,0.03].

But the control is what to read. Excluding twelve pieces the corpus has no opinion about removed a smaller share of the database and did ten times more damage — 2.1 % of baseline row-1 survival against the mined list's 22.4 %. So the ranking is not arbitrary: it found pieces the low rows can genuinely spare, and spent more of the database for a tenth of the cost. What failed was the dose, not the statistics. §06 has the numbers, §07 what to do instead.

01 · the design

Four sides, one frame

The frame pins four corner pieces and four corner clues. That is a lot of constraint: only a few pieces can sit beside a given corner piece and still leave room for the clue two cells in. So placement near a corner is nowhere near uniform — and it differs between the four corners, because they carry different pieces and different clues. That is the signal.

The beamer grows bottom-up and fills eleven rows, so one run only ever sees a band. The same frame is therefore run from all four sides and each side's boards are turned back onto canonical coordinates. The board is partitioned into nine zones on the bands [0–4] [5–10] [11–15], and at --stop_row 10 those are exactly the cut points where the four bands land:

side 0  rows  0..10        side 2  rows  5..15
side 1  cols  5..15        side 3  cols  0..10

So every zone is wholly inside a side's band or wholly outside it, never half-covered — and each corner zone is seen by exactly two sides: BL [0, 3], BR [0, 1], TL [2, 3], TR [1, 2].

why exposure is the whole problem

Side 0 fills rows 0–10 and therefore cannot place anything in the top-left or top-right zone. Count naively and every piece looks like it avoids the top — an artefact of where the beam was pointed, not a fact about the puzzle. So each lift is computed per side over only the zones that side covers, and pooled afterwards across the sides that cover it.

02 · replication

Do independent views agree?

Two sides see each corner, using different random borders, a different RNG stream and a different search direction. What they do share is the frame — the same pinned corner piece, the same clue two cells in — and that is the conditioning the whole experiment is about. What they do not share is the search. So agreement means the frame is driving the placement; disagreement would mean the heuristic is, and no further analysis would rescue it.

One honest qualification. Each corner is reached early in the growth of both sides that see it — within four rows or four columns. That is the regime where the border and the clues dominate and the objective has barely begun to matter, so the agreement below is strongest exactly where constraint is strongest. That is the effect this experiment set out to find rather than a flaw in it, but it does mean the numbers describe the constrained neighbourhood of a corner, not the board at large.

Mean Spearman across the four corner zones: +0.701. Under the same shuffle the correlation is +0.006, which is what “no structure” looks like.

03 · what the corners want

The preferences themselves

A lift of 2.0× means the piece lands in that zone twice as often as an average piece of its kind does. Edge and inner pieces have separate baselines: an edge piece can only sit on the frame, so comparing it against inner pieces would measure the frame, not a preference.

246 of 247 pieces have at least one zone whose 95 % bootstrap interval clears 1.00×. Run the identical procedure on corpora where piece labels have been shuffled within each board, and it returns 51 (range 39–69 over 12 replicates) — that is the multiplicity of 247 pieces across nine zones leaking through, and the observed count is 4.8× it.

Two things in that figure are worth more than the diagonal. The first is the red opposite the blue: pieces that prefer the bottom-left actively avoid the top-right, and vice versa. A piece does not merely have a corner, it has an anti-corner — which is exactly what makes the far-side score below possible.

The second is what is missing. Almost no piece prefers BM, ML, MR or TM, the four edge zones. The sorting is into corners and centre, not into nine regions. The corners are where the pinned pieces are, and the constraint evidently does not propagate sideways along an edge the way it propagates into a corner.

04 · the mechanism

Why a piece prefers a corner

A piece cannot prefer a corner for its own sake. It prefers it because the colours it carries are the ones that corner's pinned pieces demand, and because the pieces that fit beside those pieces demand others in turn. Colour is 22 buckets against 256, so it is far better estimated than the piece level — if the piece-level pattern is real, there should be a colour pattern under it.

05 · the actionable part

Pieces the beam should not be spending

The beamer grows bottom-up. Run it in the canonical frame to --stop_row 12 and rows 13–15 are unreachable, so a piece that belongs up there is budget the search is wasting. The score is

far_score = log2( lift(rows 13-15) / lift(rows 0-2) )

bootstrapped over borders. Only pieces whose whole interval sits above zero qualify — evidence of a far-side preference, not a point estimate that happens to be positive. 90 pieces clear that bar.

the ceiling, and it is not statistical

Rows 1–14 hold 14×14 = 196 inner cells and the puzzle has exactly 196 inner pieces. There are no spares. A beam to row 12 places 168 of them and two more are reserved for the row-13 clues, leaving 26 spare. Exclude K pieces and the slack drops to 26−K; push K toward the slack and the run collapses however good the statistics are. The list is capped at 13 — half the slack — for that reason alone.

read this before using the list

The three sides that see rows 13–15 do not agree on this score (sides 1–2: +0.417, sides 1–3: -0.075, sides 2–3: +0.391; mean +0.244). The zone preferences above replicate; this particular ranking does not yet. Treat the exclusion list as a hypothesis the A/B test is about to judge, not as a finding.

06 · the test

Does acting on it work?

Everything above is description. This is the only part that decides anything: the beamer run twice in the canonical frame, identical except that one arm bars the 12 far-side pieces.

why this does not count emitted boards

At --stop_row 12 with every clue on, this machine emits essentially nothing — the beam dies before it gets there on all but a freak border, so counting emissions would compare zero against zero. Both arms therefore run --verbose, and the comparison uses the per-row line the beam prints on the way up: uniq, the number of distinct states surviving the dedup at that row. It is continuous, recorded for every border at every row it reaches, and it is what “the search still has room” means.

The arms are not paired. You would expect the same seed to give both the same borders, but the border sampler ranks candidates by fan-out into the chain database, and excluding pieces changes that database — so the two runs diverge from the first border. The comparison is between two rates over thousands of borders.

Survival intervals are Wilson per arm and Newcombe on the difference; the width ratio is bootstrapped over borders. The verdict reads row 10 — the deepest row where both arms still have enough borders to estimate a median.

the database cost of removing a piece

A chain record holds five pieces and needs all five available, so the database shrinks as roughly the fifth power of the surviving piece fraction. Removing 12 of 194 searchable inner pieces — 6.2 % of them — predicts a 1 − 0.9385 = 27 % chain loss and delivers 22 %: 2,730,016,036 records down to 2,137,097,200. A 6 % cut in pieces buys a 22 % cut in chains, and the clue-pinned rows have the fewest viable chains to begin with.

That is why the dose was too large. It is not why this particular list failed — see below.

Was it these pieces, or any twelve pieces?

The result above cannot tell “we picked the wrong pieces” from “excluding pieces is the wrong mechanism”. So a third arm excludes twelve pieces the corpus calls undecided — far-side interval straddling zero, no evidence either way. It is the cleanest control available: same dose, same mechanism, no information.

excluded setchains leftdatabase lost row-1 survivalfraction of baseline kept
none (baseline)2,730,016,036 — 32.17 % 100 %
12 far-side (mined)2,137,097,200 21.7 % 7.23 % 22.5 %
12 undecided (control)2,317,226,804 15.1 % 0.69 % 2.1 %
the result that matters most here

The control removed fewer chains — 15.1 % against 21.7 % — and did ten times more damage, leaving 2.1 % of baseline row-1 survival against 22.5 %.

So database size does not explain the damage, and the mined list is not an arbitrary one. The corpus identified pieces the low rows can genuinely spare: it gave up a larger share of the database for a tenth of the cost. The ranking has real predictive content. What was wrong was the dose — twelve pieces is far past what the clue rows can absorb, whichever twelve they are.

07 · what to try instead

The statistics survived; the delivery did not

The ranking works; the delivery was too blunt. A hard database exclusion removes chains at the fifth power of the piece fraction, and twelve pieces is past what the clue rows can absorb. Three ways to spend the finding more cheaply, in the order I would try them:

  • Make it a score term, not a ban. The beam already ranks candidates by a colour objective; a small penalty for placing a far-side piece in a low row would bias selection without removing a single chain from the database. The pieces stay available when a row genuinely needs them, which is exactly what the clue rows turned out to require.
  • Give it to Stage C instead. The backtracker and the CP-SAT tools have no chain database, so a piece-to-region prior costs them nothing structural — it is just move ordering. The corner preferences are strongest near the corners, which is where the tail solvers do their work.
  • Re-run the exclusion at a dose of two or three, not twelve. This is now the most promising of the three, because the control showed the ranking works — it was the quantity that broke the clue rows. Chain loss goes as the fifth power of the piece fraction, so three pieces costs about 7 % of the database against 22 % for twelve, and the far-side score's top two or three are exactly the ones its intervals are most confident about.
08 · the question this did not answer

Few boards may be the point, not the problem

The A/B above measured P(board emitted). It did not measure P(completable | emitted), and those are different questions. Stage C is the bottleneck, not Stage B — there are already thousands of high-scoring partials and no way to focus on the few worth CP-SAT time. If exclusion yields few boards that are far more completable, that is a win nothing above could have seen.

The mechanism is a real blind spot. The beam's objective scores colour supply, not which specific pieces remain. A board can finish row 11 with a perfect colour ledger and still be unfinishable, because it spent the only pieces that could ever sit at some cell in row 14. Exclusion closes that by brute force.

But the corpus says the property may not need forcing at all. Over 14,720 side-0 boards, counting how many of the 12 far-side pieces each one left unplaced:

two numbers that change the design

The beam already leaves 4.37 of 12 unplaced against 3.46 expected under indifferent placement, and 2.6% of boards leave eight or more. Elite boards therefore already exist in ordinary output, and selecting them costs zero search time — where forcing the property cost roughly 100× the throughput.

And 83% of the variance is decided board by board, not by the border (17% between borders). You cannot pick good borders for this; you have to pick good boards. Which also means --max_per_config is working against you here — it caps exactly the distribution you would want to sample deeply.

09 · before any of this reaches Stage C

The prior does not transfer as measured

The study's frame is orientation 0 with corners BL=3 BR=2 TL=0 TR=1. Checked against the real boards in data/: not one matches it, and most carry no clue commitment at all — they came from free runs. Three of the four boards in best_463.csv satisfy zero clues, and every one uses a different corner assignment.

So a prior phrased as “piece 124 prefers the top-right of the published board” is unusable on that corpus. The fix costs nothing: the preference is not really about board geometry, it is about which pinned pieces a corner carries. In this frame TR holds corner-piece 1, BL holds 3, BR holds 2, TL holds 0 — so re-key the whole table to

piece 124 wants the corner occupied by corner-piece 1

which is frame-independent, because the four corner pieces are identifiable in any board. Caveat worth carrying: each corner here is anchored by both a corner piece and a nearby clue, so re-keying keeps the corner anchor and drops the clue anchor. Expect the transferred prior to be weaker than the measured one — and that is measurable, by re-running the replication check keyed that way.

10 · an aside worth keeping

Where the beam actually dies

Measured across the farm: of every 100 borders the sweep tries, about 96 die at row 1 or 2 — the two rows the clues pin. Of the four that survive row 2, 98 % reach row 10. The survival curve is a cliff followed by a plateau.

That reframes what an exclusion list can do. Rows 3–10 are close to free; the search is not slowly grinding down, it is being killed at the clue-pinned rows and then coasting. So a piece list helps or hurts mainly through what it does to rows 1–2, and the danger is real: taking pieces away can only make those rows harder to thread. That is why the test reports survival per row as well as frontier width — a list that buys width at row 11 by costing survival at row 2 is a bad trade, and the two columns show it separately.

11 · limits

What this does not show

  • These are the beam's habits, not the puzzle's truth. The heuristic has its own taste and the corpus inherits it. Cross-side replication is what separates the two, and it is a correlation, not a proof.
  • The corner assignment is a bet. No clue pins a corner, so the four corner pieces can fill the four corners 4! = 24 ways and only one is the solution's. Everything near the border is conditioned on that choice; the centre barely notices.
  • Nothing here transfers to the production beamer, which hedges across all four orientations and samples its own corners. The exclusion list is specific to this frame.
  • No board in the corpus is a solution. The statistics describe where a partial-board search puts pieces when it survives eleven rows, which is related to, but not the same as, where they belong.
  • The zone preferences replicate far better than the far-side ranking does. Two sides agree about a corner at ρ ≈ 0.70; the three sides that see rows 13–15 agree about the far-side score much more weakly, and one pair disagrees outright. The corner result and the exclusion list do not stand or fall together.

Corpus: corpus.csv · 55,712 boards from 1,741 borders — side 0: 460 · side 1: 428 · side 2: 415 · side 3: 438
